title: Pauri 33, sound: aakhan jor
tomorrow: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own

segments.voice: Yesterday: pavarreeaa, the steps, and your line, step by step. Today, the next rung, sound first.

Ever tried not to laugh? A quiet classroom, a serious meeting, a moment when laughing is the worst thing you could do. And it rises anyway. You bite your cheek, you stare at the floor, and your shoulders shake. Or the opposite: you want to say the right thing to a grieving friend, and nothing comes out at all. Speaking and staying quiet look like the two things a person controls best. Pauri 33 opens with exactly those two, and one hard little word that keeps coming back like a hammer.
screen: `TRYING NOT TO LAUGH.` → `THE WORDS THAT WON'T COME.` → `ONE WORD, LIKE A HAMMER.`

segments.voice: The first line: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor. Four sounds. Aakhan: speaking, saying; it echoes aakheeah from yesterday, where the Name was said on a million tongues. Jor: power, force, strength, still alive in everyday Punjabi when people mean push hard, put your strength into it. Chupai: in silence; you may know chup from Punjabi, as in chup kar, be quiet. Nah: not, no. So: no power to speak, no power to keep silent. Commentators read that nah across both halves. Now the shape. Jor lands at the end of each half: two short beats, then the heavy one. The next line flips it, so jor comes first and last: jor na mangan, den na jor. No power to ask, no power to give. The word boxes the line in. The whole stanza keeps doing this: jor ten times in eight short lines, nine of them with na or nah beside it, like knocking on door after door and finding each one locked. Tomorrow, which doors, and whose hand holds the key. Today, feel the hammer. You can almost recite this stanza by its rhythm alone.
screen: `AAKHAN — SPEAKING.` · `JOR — POWER, FORCE.` · `CHUPAI NAH JOR — NOR TO BE SILENT.` · `JOR, AGAIN AND AGAIN, LIKE A HAMMER.` · then, large: `AAKHAN JOR.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud three times, slowly, letting jor land heavy like a hand on a table: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor; then the next one, jor na mangan, den na jor. Then stop speaking and simply stay silent. Even the silence isn't quite yours, since thoughts keep talking; don't fight them, let them knock and pass.
Chupai, silence. It opens: aakhan jor, chupai nah jor, no power to speak, no power to be silent, and the word jor keeps coming back like a hammer.
Your line: aakhan jor. Even speech and silence aren't fully in our power. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 218 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 33, MEANING: NO POWER OF OUR OWN.`

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 33's repeated word jor, power, gives it a strong, hammering rhythm.

chat.says: What does 'aakhan jor, chupai nah jor' mean?
options: No power to speak, none to keep silent. Even speech and silence aren't fully ours.
Speak with power when you can, and stay silent whenever you have none.
Words have great power, so it's always better to just stay silent.
chat.meaning: Aakhan is speaking, chupai is in silence, jor is power, and nah means not: no power to speak, none to be silent.
